newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-JONES SAYS HE DOESN'T HAVE TO RESTORE HIS REPUTATION.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-JONES SAYS HE DOESN'T HAVE TO RESTORE HIS REPUTATION.

text.p: Roy Jones, Jr. says
he does not have to restore his reputation as the world's best
"pound for pound" fighter in his rematch with World Boxing
Council light heavyweight champion Montell Griffin Thursday.
Jones says his loss to Griffin by disqualification after
hitting the challenger twice when he was already down on one
knee in the ninth round of their first title fight on March 21
has not tarnished his reputation.
"I know that I am the best "pound for pound" fighter in
the world," says the 34-1 Jones, who has held titles in the
middleweight, super middleweight and light heavyweight
divisions. "I have a loss, but who beat me? I have a loss by
disqualification."
Since their first fight in Atlantic City, Jones has blamed
the referee for the sequence of events that ended the bout
with Griffin face down on the canvas and unable to continue.
Jones says referee Tony Perez should have quickly stepped
between the fighters and sent Jones to a neutral corner when
Griffin went to one knee to take a respite after absorbing a
barrage of blows.
"It was the ref's fault more than mine," says Jones.
"When you are down whose job is it to call you are down,
the referee's. When you make a touchdown or go offsides it's
not your job to make the call it's the referee's," said Jones,
ignoring that boxing is different than football and everyone
knows a boxer is not to hit a man when he is down.
"It's my job to go out there and box and not to consider
when a guy is down," says Jones.
So adamant is Jones that what he did was correct, that he
warned of doing the same again Thursday.
"It can happen again," says Jones. "If he (the referee)
doesn't step in and stop it, it will happen again."
Jones' actions in the ring and his continual refusal to
acknowledge that he did anything wrong has left Griffin
simmering with anger.
"I'm coming in there angry with a lot of built in rage
because I just want to get the man back in the ring for doing
what he did," says Griffin, 27-0. "He hit me with a cheap shot
that was seen all over the nation and every time I see it I
get upset, that's what I'm basing my thing on.
"I did lose a little respect for him," Griffin says of the
28-year-old Jones. "Any man who does anything cheap to anybody
you got to lose a little respect. The man was supposed to be
the best pound for pound fighter. Why did he have to do that?
He was worried, frustrated, that's why he did what he did. You
can't but lose respect for him."
Griffin's indignation at what happened is compounded by
his feeling that he would have beaten Jones if the fight had
continued.
"Of course, I feel cheated," says Griffin, who was leading
on one scorecard and was narrowly trailing on the other two.
"There is still a question up in the air because the fight
never got to finish the 12 rounds. A lot of questions will be
answered."
"I've done nothing differnt in training camp, I was
winning the fight why should I change," says Jones, who
pursued his passion of basketball by playing for the
Jacksonville Barracudas of the United States Basketball League
through the end of June.
While there has been a change in Griffin's training camp
routine after Hall of Fame trainer Eddie Futch left his corner
in a dispute over money.
"I found out that I could beat him in any phase of the
game," Griffin, 27, said.
"I was out jabbing him from the outside. Whenever he threw
a punch I countered and landed. You look at his face he was
busted up.
"Everything that never happened to him in his career
happened that night," says Jones. "I can't but have confidence
in myself."
